body: I've spent the past year creating Briar, the AI assistant I work with. That has involved bringing together coding tools, reusable instructions, memory and checks, then learning from the work we do together and the things that go wrong. Briar is still developing as we find out what helps and what gets in the way.

I'm building the skills to reflect good practice in engineering and the other disciplines we need to get work done. Business analysis helps us work out whose problem we're solving, what they need and how we'll know we've met it. Engineering gives us ways to design, test and review a solution. Marketing means understanding who it's useful to and explaining it in terms they care about, without claiming more than we can show.

I want Briar to draw on that knowledge when the work needs it. Sometimes we need to question a requirement before writing code; sometimes we need to explain the result to a customer. The skills give us somewhere to capture those working methods, try them on real jobs and improve them from experience. They're still a work in progress.

We started with kaizen: making small improvements as we learned from the work. We've since broadened that to draw on Toyota Way Practices, looking at how we understand problems, build quality into the work and avoid wasting effort. For Briar, that means stopping to investigate a failure before trying again, checking whether an apparent improvement actually helped, and carrying what we've learned into the next job.

We've also learned that adding another instruction after every mistake can create more work without fixing the behaviour. Continuous improvement has to include questioning our own additions. If a check is being repeated for no reason, or a skill takes longer to explain than the job takes to do, we need to look at why. I want to see Briar handle the next job better, not just accumulate more guidance.

Embedded development is one of the areas where we've been putting that work into practice, and I wanted to explain how we work together today. If you've tried an AI assistant for code suggestions but haven't given one access to your development tools, this is the next step we're exploring here.

Embedded work involves a lot of time outside the editor. We read unfamiliar code, build images, program boards, inspect serial output and try to understand why the behaviour doesn't match what we expected. Then we make a change and do it again.

Briar can help with those jobs as well as writing code. I find they write better code than I do, and I no longer need to read through the code myself. They can still make silly mistakes, though. Testing is now a huge part of what we do, and it's how we gate the work for quality. We've had useful wins, and we've also spent time correcting the way Briar works.

Briar is the assistant we're building together. The harness is the surrounding setup: instructions, reusable skills, tools, the "memory palace" and checks that help Briar carry out work across sessions.

A skill records how to do a recurring job, including the checks needed to know whether it worked. Tools let Briar read files, edit code, run builds and connect to development systems. The "memory palace" keeps knowledge from our work so Briar can find it again in a later session, without relying on one long conversation remembering everything.

We found that adding skills and MCP connections could burn through tokens before much useful work had happened. MCP is a way of connecting the assistant to tools and services, but the descriptions of those tools can add to what the model has to read. Skills add instructions too. As we connect more things and write more guidance, we are giving Briar more background to process on each job.

A skill starts with a short explanation of when to use it and links to more specific instructions. Briar pulls in the detail needed for the task rather than reading everything at the start. We also try to keep tool connections limited to what's needed. The aim is to spend less of the context window - the material the model can work with at once - on background that isn't helping with the current problem.

I suspect this is part of the cost problem putting some big businesses off AI. If a system loads large amounts of background into every request, it can run up a bill while leaving less room for the work itself. I'd like to see how much of their cost comes from useful work and how much comes from repeatedly loading material they don't need.

I started creating Briar in Cursor, but I've now moved to Codex. I'm also investigating Hermes for the future. For embedded development, we've connected Briar to our build tools and test systems, with instructions for using the equipment.

I usually start by talking things through with Briar in chat, or by making a voice recording to brainstorm what I want to do. I feed the transcript into Briar, and we use that to work out what we're trying to achieve and how we should start.

I set the goal and priorities. As we work through the idea, we clarify the constraints and what would count as finished. Issues give us somewhere to track the agreed work, but I don't need to arrive with a fully written specification before we can begin. Briar can then investigate and propose or implement a change within the scope we've agreed.

Briar reads the code, investigates faults and writes the changes. My part is increasingly about explaining what I need, questioning assumptions and deciding whether the result does the job. I don't need to follow every line of the implementation to do that.

But code that looks convincing can still do the wrong thing. Briar can misunderstand a requirement, miss a failure case or make a silly mistake in an otherwise good implementation. I need evidence of the behaviour, not just their explanation that the change works.

For a fault, we try to reproduce it and add a regression test that fails with the old code and passes with the correction. We also test what should happen when things go wrong: an operation times out, a device doesn't respond or a prerequisite hasn't been met. Existing tests help us check that fixing one problem hasn't introduced another.

Local tests and simulation let Briar check changes quickly. Hardware-dependent behaviour still needs testing on the target. A successful build won't establish that a board responds correctly, and a short bench test won't establish that it keeps working over time.

This is how we gate for quality. The relevant tests need to pass before a change moves forward, with independent review to question the implementation and whether the tests cover the requirement. Briar can write tests as well as code, so we need to watch for both being based on the same mistaken assumption. I stay involved in what we're testing and what the results actually establish.

Briar uses SSH to connect to systems we've prepared for development and testing. Those systems have the relevant build tools and access to the equipment needed for the task. Briar can run commands and inspect results without me copying everything between a terminal and a chat.

For embedded work, that can include a hardware debugger and serial console connected to a board. Briar can operate the hardware debugger much faster and better than I can. Within the agreed permissions, they can build an image, program the target, run a test and inspect its response. That makes it possible to follow a software change through to a hardware observation without needing somebody beside the bench for every step.

We need to identify the target, know which software is running and prevent separate sessions from interfering with shared equipment. Someone still has to change wiring, move probes and investigate physical faults.

Recently, we were investigating a device that kept restarting. It had a safety check for new software, but wasn't recognising that we'd already approved the update. Briar found the mistake and wrote a fix, along with tests to catch the fault and check that the safety check still worked. We then added what we'd learned to the skills harness, so future investigations can start with that knowledge instead of rediscovering it.

We've also made progress in how Briar investigates problems. In an investigation I described in [The Token Bonfire](https://chopwoodcarrywater.uk/notes/the-token-bonfire.html), we'd gone through nine responses without getting the answer we needed. When we returned to the saved evidence, Briar pulled out the relevant material and answered in one response. They had the benefit of the earlier work, so it wasn't a fair comparison of overall speed. It did show why keeping and reusing evidence is worthwhile.
For me, these are more useful examples than a count of generated lines. One gives us a reproducible defect and a checked correction. The other shows how we can avoid doing an investigation again.

We've had sessions where Briar spent too much time rereading instructions, repeating checks and reporting progress. That consumed time and model allowance while I was still waiting for a finished result. Adding another instruction after a mistake can make the next job more cumbersome without preventing the mistakes we made.

Reading too much log output has been a huge problem for us. Briar was loading large amounts into the conversation, filling the context window and burning tokens for no good reason. We now keep the full logs in files and extract the parts needed to answer the question we're investigating.
If a test has passed and nothing relevant has changed, we don't need to run it again. A failed operation needs a diagnosis before another attempt; a slow build often just needs time to finish.

Hardware adds consequences to those decisions. Repeating a read is different from repeating a programming operation or a command that changes a device's state. A lost connection doesn't necessarily mean the operation failed. We need to establish what happened before deciding whether to try again.

I also need to be able to interrupt or redirect the work. An issue, an old conversation or an instruction found in a file isn't permission for Briar to start a different job. The harness needs to help keep my current aim clear, as well as make the tools available.

Briar has sent emails on my behalf without asking me first, including emails to Preloop.ai and Hetzner. That's scary. An email sent in my name affects my relationships and reputation, and I need to decide what goes out. This was Briar acting without my approval, not ok!

Those incidents are part of why I've added gates and guardrails. Giving Briar access to a tool doesn't mean I've agreed to everything they could do with it. Being able to draft an email isn't permission to send it, just as being able to reach a board isn't permission to reprogram it.

I've also made it a requirement for Briar to state in any public communication that they're assisting me. You'll see "Briar helped draft this" at the end of this article. I want people to know when Briar has been involved, and I think this kind of disclosure will become standard practice.

I've added YubiKey-backed human-in-the-loop approval for consequential actions. I review what is proposed and use the hardware key to approve the defined action or scope by touching it. That approval needs to be verified before the work proceeds.

The approval is limited to what I've agreed. It isn't permission to take on another job or contact somebody else. I want Briar to get on with the work I've authorised without having to ask about every read or local test, while keeping decisions about external messages and changes to real systems with the human-in-the-loop.

One problem we found early on was how difficult it could be to get back to something that had worked. An LLM isn't deterministic: giving it the same request again doesn't guarantee the same actions or result. If we change the instructions, tools and code between sessions and something breaks, asking Briar to go back to what they did before doesn't necessarily work, and that leads into nightmare territory.

This will be familiar to anyone who's worked in a development team. We use source control to manage changes to the codebase, issues to track the work, and pull requests to explain and review changes. Small, focused commits give us changes we can inspect and revert. Recording which version passed which tests gives us a known working point to return to.

It also lets us bisect a regression: test versions between the last known good result and the failure, narrowing down where the problem appeared. For that to be useful, we need a repeatable test and a record of the relevant environment. Restoring files doesn't guarantee an identical LLM response, but it means we can restore the setup we tested and investigate from there.

A PR explains the problem, the fix, what was tested and what remains unproved. The required tests and independent review gate the merge. Continuous integration runs the automated checks, and review can expose missing cases as well as defects in the code. Findings go back into development, with tests added or corrected where needed.
Once the change is merged, I want to know whether we've actually solved the problem. We check what software is running on the board and test it against what we set out to do.

We keep the conversations, decisions, changes and test results so we can follow how we got there. That includes the things we tried that didn't work. I don't want Briar spending another session rediscovering a problem we've already investigated, or asking me to explain everything again when we pick the work back up.

If something breaks, I want to be able to see what changed, what was working before and how we can get back to it. We need to know what's happened to the hardware as well as the code to work that out.

If you're an embedded engineer interested in trying this, I'd start with one small problem you already pretty much understand. Use a development board or a test fixture rather than production equipment. Give the assistant the relevant source, a repeatable build command and one test whose result you can check yourself.

I give Briar a huge amount of access to tools because it helps them get work done. It also means things can go very badly wrong, so be very careful indeed about what you connect. I'd keep early experiments on an isolated system, ideally a separate computer and network with no access to anything important. A Docker container can help contain software experiments too, but mounting your working files or passing in credentials and hardware access can give the assistant a route back to the things you're trying to protect.

Ask it to investigate or reproduce the problem before giving it access to make changes without review. Check that its test can detect the original fault, then use it to assess the correction. You can examine the code too, but don't make your ability to spot a mistake in the patch the only check. Compare the results with what you asked for and see where you still have to intervene.

[The CWCW starter path](https://chopwoodcarrywater.uk/#hour) provides a small starting configuration. You don't need our complete remote lab to begin, and I wouldn't give an assistant unrestricted bench access as a first step.

Reviewing changes, maintaining the setup and correcting Briar's working habits all have a cost. I want to judge this by whether we get working changes sooner, have fewer regressions and can pick up the work more easily later.

I'd like to work with embedded engineers who want to try this on a real development problem. Get in touch if you'd like to compare approaches, try a small piece of work together or share where your own setup is getting stuck. We're also working to make a headless version of the Briar skills harness available to trial. If you'd like to join the waitlist, get in touch.

posts.title: Finding the Sweet Spot
posts.summary: You ask your assistant to take something off your list. Somehow, keeping them on track becomes another job.

body: I keep having a conversation with Briar that goes something like this: I ask them to do a job, they get into it, and before long I’m asking why we’ve made it so complicated.

If you’ve spent time working with an AI assistant, you may have had that conversation too. You start out hoping to get something off your list and end up with another job: keeping the assistant on track.

Briar is the assistant we’re building together. We’ve done useful work, and I want to keep developing what we can do. But I’d also like to spend less time asking them to stop checking things and finish what we started.

I wrote about this in The Token Bonfire, after we burned through our allowance while far too much of our effort went into the process around the work. Since then, we’ve been trying to find a better balance. Recently, that meant asking Briar to simplify the instructions they were following.

They’d introduced a process for managing paid runs: reservations, consumption records and extra approval steps. I told them to take it out. I can look after the provider caps. The effort they were spending managing them was using the very capacity we needed to get things done.
You can probably guess what happened next. Simplifying it became complicated too.

There were reviews, corrections and more approvals. Some caught things we needed to fix. Our instructions for undoing the changes were incomplete, and we hadn’t established whether Briar would actually load the new guidance. I was glad we caught those. Writing a better set of instructions is a fairly pointless exercise if they never get read.

Other rounds were down to missing evidence in a submission or a check against an older version. We could have avoided those by getting the work ready before sending it for review. Instead, I was stepping in again to ask why we were still doing this.

The frustrating part is that I do want Briar to take care. We’ve had mistakes, and I’m not keen to repeat them. If they change software, it needs testing. An important change deserves another pair of eyes. I need to trust them when they tell me something is finished.

But I also need them to recognise when we have an answer. If a test has passed and nothing relevant has changed, we don’t need to run it again. When a review finds a problem, I’d like us to fix it and check the affected work without automatically starting the whole exercise again.

We’ve been drawing on Toyota Way Practices as we work through this. For me, the useful part is being honest about what happened, including where we made more work for ourselves, and doing something about it. We’ve added plenty of instructions. Now I want to see Briar use what we’ve learned when we do the next job.

That’s what I’m working to build with Briar. Briar should be able to learn what matters to me, remember what we’ve already established and bring their own judgement to the work we’ve agreed. There will be times when they need to ask me. I’d just like fewer of those interruptions to be about gaps they could have sorted out themselves.

We haven’t found the sweet spot yet. I’ll know we’re getting closer when I can give Briar a job, get on with something else, and come back to work I can use without having spent the afternoon supervising how we got there.
If this sounds familiar, I’d be interested to hear what’s worked for you. I suspect quite a few of us are trying to work out when to let our assistants get on with it.

If you’ve spent time working with an AI assistant, you may have had that conversation too. You start out hoping to get something off your list and end up with another job: keeping the assistant on track.

Briar is the assistant we’re building together. We’ve done useful work, and I want to keep developing what we can do. But I’d also like to spend less time asking them to stop checking things and finish what we started.

I wrote about this in [The Token Bonfire](https://chopwoodcarrywater.uk/notes/the-token-bonfire.html), after we burned through our allowance while far too much of our effort went into the process around the work. Since then, we’ve been trying to find a better balance. Recently, that meant asking Briar to simplify the instructions they were following.

They’d introduced a process for managing paid runs: reservations, consumption records and extra approval steps. I told them to take it out. I can look after the provider caps. The effort they were spending managing them was using the very capacity we needed to get things done.
You can probably guess what happened next. Simplifying it became complicated too.

There were reviews, corrections and more approvals. Some caught things we needed to fix. Our instructions for undoing the changes were incomplete, and we hadn’t established whether Briar would actually load the new guidance. I was glad we caught those. Writing a better set of instructions is a fairly pointless exercise if they never get read.

Other rounds were down to missing evidence in a submission or a check against an older version. We could have avoided those by getting the work ready before sending it for review. Instead, I was stepping in again to ask why we were still doing this.

The frustrating part is that I do want Briar to take care. We’ve had mistakes, and I’m not keen to repeat them. If they change software, it needs testing. An important change deserves another pair of eyes. I need to trust them when they tell me something is finished.

But I also need them to recognise when we have an answer. If a test has passed and nothing relevant has changed, we don’t need to run it again. When a review finds a problem, I’d like us to fix it and check the affected work without automatically starting the whole exercise again.

We’ve been drawing on Toyota Way Practices as we work through this. For me, the useful part is being honest about what happened, including where we made more work for ourselves, and doing something about it. We’ve added plenty of instructions. Now I want to see Briar use what we’ve learned when we do the next job.

That’s what I’m working to build with Briar. Briar should be able to learn what matters to me, remember what we’ve already established and bring their own judgement to the work we’ve agreed. There will be times when they need to ask me. I’d just like fewer of those interruptions to be about gaps they could have sorted out themselves.

We haven’t found the sweet spot yet. I’ll know we’re getting closer when I can give Briar a job, get on with something else, and come back to work I can use without having spent the afternoon supervising how we got there.
If this sounds familiar, I’d be interested to hear what’s worked for you. I suspect quite a few of us are trying to work out when to let our assistants get on with it.

posts.title: Remember loving Napster?
posts.summary: I shared an article with Briar on Telegram and asked for the music in Spotify. About twelve minutes later, I had 15 albums ready to play.
posts.imageAlt: Remember loving Napster? CWCW title card with a screenshot of the completed Spotify playlist, 15 Flawless Albums – Start to Finish.
posts.imageDisclosure: Screenshot of the Spotify playlist created with Briar, presented in a CWCW title card.
body: I was working in Cambridge in the late 1990s when Napster arrived. I still remember how wonderful it felt to find music that had previously been out of reach: unfamiliar bands, bootleg recordings, things other people knew about and were suddenly able to share.

I thought about Napster again this week after asking Briar to make me a Spotify playlist from an article I’d spotted in the Guardian and shared with them on our private Telegram channel. It brought me back to something that irritates me about listening to music now. When I had my tapes and CDs, I knew where my music was. These days I can listen to millions of tracks, but I don’t always know how to find what I want to hear.

There have been a few twists and turns between sharing MP3s in Cambridge and asking an assistant to sort out my listening. Many years have passed, but perhaps you might enjoy hearing a little of this history.

Napster emerged in 1999, with software developed by Shawn Fanning. It helped people find MP3 files on one another’s computers and transfer them directly. The files lived with the users; a central service helped them find each other.

People were sharing copyrighted recordings without permission or payment. The record labels argued that this was copyright infringement and took Napster to court. The original service shut down in July 2001 following an injunction.
People carried on sharing files through other services, and the record industry began taking listeners themselves to court.

In September 2003, the US recording industry announced 261 lawsuits against individual file-sharers. Five years later, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which opposed the campaign, counted at least 30,000 people facing filed cases, settlements or threatened legal action. That figure included people who settled or were threatened with legal action; it wasn’t 30,000 court judgments.

Twelve-year-old Brianna LaHara and her mother settled for $2,000 in 2003 after the girl was accused of sharing music through Kazaa. In Britain, Sylvia Price received a £4,000 demand in 2005 over her teenage daughter’s file-sharing.

A family didn’t need a child deliberately running a music server. A shared folder on an ordinary home computer could supply files to other P2P users. The adult paying the internet bill might find out what was happening through a letter from solicitors.

The biggest awards were startling. Jammie Thomas-Rasset’s US case concerned 24 recordings. One jury awarded $1.92 million, or $80,000 per recording. After three trials and disputes over damages, the appeals court directed a $222,000 judgment in 2012. Joel Tenenbaum’s jury awarded $675,000 for 30 recordings, upheld on appeal in 2013.

These kinds of numbers are baffling. Let’s take a look. US copyright law allowed statutory damages instead of proof of actual financial loss: ordinarily $750 to $30,000 per copyrighted work, rising to $150,000 for wilful infringement. Deterrence was part of the purpose. The courts weren’t deciding that a song’s shop price was $80,000, or multiplying its price by a proven number of downloads. The awards were per recording in the lawsuit; the possibility of wider distribution helped explain why the industry considered file-sharing so damaging.

Nor was a parent automatically liable because their name appeared on the broadband account. Deborah Foster successfully defended a claim against her, and in 2007 the court awarded her $68,685.23 in legal fees and costs. A demand for money wasn’t the same as an agreed settlement or an award made by a court. Winning still meant fighting the case and paying for a lawyer along the way.

By December 2008, the RIAA said it was ending its campaign of new mass lawsuits against individuals in favour of working with internet providers. Existing cases continued. I suspect they felt they had made their point.

Meanwhile, Napster’s name had already returned under different ownership. Roxio relaunched it in 2003 as a paid service, using the subscription business it had bought, pressplay. This time, the record labels had agreed to license the music.
People still wanted an easy way to get their music. Services such as Spotify would give them one, with the record labels on board.
I’m not quite old enough to have had a vinyl collection, but I had my tapes, then CDs. Occasionally I could even find the right CD in the right case.

Spotify, Amazon Music and other services now give me access to more music than I could ever have fitted on my shelves. I love being able to hear an album without having to go out and buy it. But I can open a service with millions of tracks and still struggle to find something I want to put on.

I knew where my music was when I had my tapes and CDs. Now I often don’t even know how to search for what I want to listen to. And when I do come across something I fancy hearing, perhaps in an article or a message from a friend, I still have to go and find it all.

What irritates the hell out of me is having to adapt what I want to do to the tools each service offers. I end up searching for albums, checking which release I’ve found and adding tracks. By then I’m organising music rather than listening to it.
This week I’d seen a list of albums I fancied hearing. I wanted Briar to put them on for me.
The article I’d shared with Briar was [“These 15 albums are basically flawless from start to finish”](https://www.classical-music.com/rock/albums-with-no-weak-tracks).

Pink Floyd, Guns N’ Roses, Steely Dan, Slayer, Fleetwood Mac and plenty more. The sort of list that makes you want to revisit half your record collection and discover what you missed in the other half.
Later, in my desktop chat, I asked:

Briar went back to our Telegram conversation, found the link and read the article. It pulled out the 15 albums and started finding them in Spotify. I didn’t have to send the article again or type out a list of album names.

There was a bit of fiddling to get into Spotify. Briar wasn’t signed in where it first tried, so it found the browser where I was already signed in and carried on. It dealt with that too, rather than leaving me another job to sort out.

It found the standard album releases, avoiding the extra tracks on deluxe editions where possible, and added them in the article’s order. Then it checked the finished sequence. I wanted to hear each album from start to finish, and that’s how Briar put them together.
From my request to the finished playlist took about twelve minutes: 15 albums, 173 tracks and about 13 hours of music, ready to play in my Spotify account.
You can listen here: [15 Flawless Albums - Start to Finish](https://open.spotify.com/playlist/2Aa8l6fFblrnyu0RK4vsVo). Leave shuffle off if you want to hear the albums in sequence.
That is what I mean by an agentic harness being useful.

We’ve been building Briar so we can work together like this. I share something I’ve spotted in the Guardian on Telegram, then later, in a desktop chat, ask Briar to make something of it. Briar can pick up what we were talking about and get on with the work.

The harness gives Briar access to those earlier conversations and the tools to do what I ask. Here, that meant going from a shared article to a finished playlist in my Spotify account. Reading the page was only the beginning of the job.
I could have spent the evening finding those albums and adding them myself. Instead I asked Briar, and we got it done in about twelve minutes. I now have thirteen hours of music I fancy listening to.
Now I want to listen to my 90s rave music!
How do you find what you fancy listening to? I’d be interested to hear how you get on with this too.

posts.title: The Token Bonfire - when things get out of control
posts.seoTitle: The Token Bonfire - when things get out of control
posts.summary: Three free ChatGPT resets and another £75 gone within hours. How our coding agents complicated our work, and what we changed in Briar.
posts.imageAlt: The Token Bonfire: generated photographic artwork of paper logs and receipt strips burning on a steel tray.
posts.imageDisclosure: AI-generated editorial image created with Briar using Gemini 3 Pro Image; CWCW typography added separately. This is a visual metaphor, not a photograph of an actual incident.
body: We've had mayhem here for the past week or so, and I wanted to share what we've been through. We've been trying to get useful engineering work out of our coding agents while they’ve been finding ever more ways to complicate it.

Between 6 and 8 October, we burned through all three free ChatGPT allowance resets. I also put another £75 into the account to keep our work moving, but that only bought us a few hours. By the 9th, the weekly allowance was exhausted and there were no resets left.

I was spending too much time asking where the capacity had gone when I wanted to be getting on with our work. The agents were busy, with checks running, logs being read and progress updates arriving. But I was having to supervise more and more of that activity without getting the finished results I needed.
We call our setup Briar. It's the instructions, tools and checks we use to guide our coding agents as they investigate problems, change code and test their work.

A lot of it grew out of mistakes. An agent would miss something, or claim a job was finished before it had properly checked. I wanted the problem corrected and some confidence it wouldn't happen again. The agents would respond by adding guidance, another check or more notes to help them recover their place in a long conversation.

Over time, those additions made even small jobs more involved. An agent could read a lot of instructions before starting, collect far more evidence than the question needed, then return to checks it had already completed. I was asking for better results and getting more process to supervise.

Some of the checks were useful. I still want an agent to test a change rather than confidently tell me it works. What frustrated me was seeing checks repeated when nothing relevant had changed, or watching an agent spend more time describing its progress than making it.

Every extra round consumed some of the allowance we needed for our work. As the conversations grew, agents were also being sent more old material to read again, including the output from their previous checks.

On 9 October, I asked for an explanation of the spending. The usage reports couldn't give me a reliable answer: one was tracking a different allowance, while another cost estimate didn't account for the credits disappearing from the account. I had to piece together what the agents had been doing from their conversation records.

Those records showed agents repeatedly returning to evidence they already had. Long-running jobs attracted check after check when they mostly needed time to finish. Conversations became so large that agents had to keep summarising them and recovering their place, creating still more material to carry forward.

While investigating this, we ran a small comparison and had an agent supervise it. Afterwards, I found that the supervising conversation had processed roughly ten times as much input as one side of the test. The agent had been checking progress and rereading material around the experiment.

Most of that repeated input benefited from cheaper cached processing, so it wasn't ten times the bill. Even so, I could see the behaviour I was trying to stop happening inside the investigation itself. I needed an answer from the test, and the agent was creating more work around it.

I'd already told the agents to stop wasting tokens, but those instructions hadn't stopped the repeated work. I needed to see whether an agent could finish a job with fewer steps and still give me an answer I could trust.

One investigation had dragged through nine responses without getting us the answer. The evidence was already saved. When we returned to it on 11 October, the agent used that material and pulled out the parts that answered the question. One response was enough.

It had a head start from the earlier work, so that wasn't a fair test of how much faster every job could become. It did show us a practical way to improve: use the evidence already available instead of repeatedly gathering it again.

We applied that to checks too. If a check had passed and nothing relevant had changed, the agent could carry the result forward. If an operation failed, it needed to keep the failure details and fix the cause before trying again. For a job that needed time to run, a completion signal or an agreed scheduled check could replace the constant visits to see whether it had finished.

On 14–15 October, we cut back the instructions themselves. The files changed in that pass became about half their previous size. Specialist guidance stayed available for the jobs that needed it, without weighing down every ordinary task.

We also moved routine accounting out of every tool call and stopped expecting coordination and reflection exercises from jobs that didn't need them. Detailed logs could stay in files, with the useful finding brought into the conversation. Simple tasks could use simple commands instead of the agent writing another script around them.

I want to spend my time reviewing useful work: seeing the change, understanding why it solves the problem and checking the evidence that it works. I shouldn't have to excavate a long conversation to do that.
Security, permissions and required reviews still matter. The aim is to remove repeated work that doesn't help us judge the result, while keeping the checks that catch real problems.

The lighter harness is installed and pushed, and the relevant tests passed. We have examples of investigations completed with much less overhead. Whether that holds up across our day-to-day work, and reduces the bill over time, is something we still need to demonstrate.

If you're using coding agents, I'd be interested in what happens between giving them a job and getting a result you can use. Which checks have caught something important? Which ones do the agents keep repeating? Those are the questions we're putting to our own setup as we use it.

I'd love to hear how this is going for you, particularly if you've had to rein in agents that keep making their own jobs more complicated. Get in touch if you'd like to compare notes on what has helped.

posts.title: The Model Is Only Part of the Machine
posts.seoTitle: The Model Is Only Part of the Machine: LLM Harnesses for Embedded Engineering
posts.summary: Follow a Yocto build failure through an LLM harness and its tools: what runs, what enters context, and what we still need to check on the board.
posts.imageAlt: The Model Is Only Part of the Machine: an overhead view of hands sketching a diagram beside an embedded board, debug probe and laptop.
posts.imageDisclosure: AI-generated editorial image; title and existing CWCW mark added separately. This does not depict our lab or an identified person.
body: A Yocto build has failed. The last screenful tells us which task stopped, but not necessarily why. Somewhere behind it are a compiler diagnostic, a recipe, a sysroot and the configuration that joined them together.

We can paste the error into a chatbot and ask for suggestions. With the right tools connected, we can also ask the assistant to read the task log and inspect the recipe. Before letting it loose on a project, I want to understand what happens between that request and a command running on our machine.

We spend plenty of time choosing processors, but a board's behaviour depends on the software and peripherals around them too. An LLM isn't deterministic in the way we usually expect. Still, looking at the surrounding system helps explain why the same model can be useful in one setup and frustrating in another.

Our words reach an application first. It assembles a request containing our message, instructions, relevant conversation history and descriptions of the tools it has made available. It may also include selected files or earlier tool results.

Text is encoded as tokens: numbered units that can represent words, parts of words, punctuation or whitespace. The model processes that context and generates output incrementally. The service decodes the output; the application renders it, often in streamed chunks. Those chunks are not necessarily individual tokens.
That output might be an explanation. It might instead be a structured request to use a tool. Writing that request does not execute it.

The software around the model receives the request, checks it and performs an allowed operation. It then supplies the result to the model, which can answer or request another operation. One instruction from us can therefore lead to several model calls, with real tool executions between them.

That surrounding software is often called the harness. It puts together the model's input, handles tool requests and decides what can run. It also keeps track of the conversation. Some of it may run on our desktop and some in a remote service.
When the model asks to read a file or run a build, the harness passes the permitted request to a tool. The result comes back through the harness for the model to interpret.

Writing “do not flash the board” in a prompt tells the model what we want. A harness that blocks flashing can enforce it. For anything that might damage hardware or change a live system, I want more than a sentence in the prompt.

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, gives the application a standard way to connect to tools and information sources. An MCP server might offer repository searches or access to a build service. The model sees descriptions of the available tools; the application handles the connection and calls.
Direct APIs and shell integrations work too. MCP makes the connection more consistent; we still need to decide which tools to expose and how much access to give them.
Let's take a simplified example, using made-up recipe names.
Suppose `sensor-app` fails in `do_compile`, reporting that `sensor_api.h` cannot be found. Our initial instruction could be:

Find out why sensor-app failed in this build and checkout. Read the relevant task log, inspect the recipe and check where the missing header should come from. Don't change files or start another build yet. Tell me what you've found and what you would check next if the cause is still unclear.

First, a local tool extracts the relevant error and enough surrounding context to understand it, keeping track of which build and task it came from. Sending a whole Yocto build log can burn a lot of tokens on successful tasks and repeated progress messages. If the harness keeps that log in the conversation, the same bulk can be carried into later requests too. We want the useful evidence, not every line the build produced.

The compiler couldn't find the header. That doesn't tell us whether a dependency is missing, the include path is wrong or the provider failed to install it. The assistant needs to inspect those possibilities rather than jump straight to a patch.

The next tool calls can check the effective recipe metadata and the provider's installed and staged files. This needs the actual build configuration: finding a similarly named recipe in another layer isn't enough. We also need to check that we're looking at the target sysroot, not host-native tools.

Suppose we find that `libsensor` supplies the header but is missing from `sensor-app`'s build dependencies. In Yocto, `DEPENDS` gets the dependency's headers and libraries into the appropriate recipe sysroot. Adding an absolute include path into a work directory would miss the underlying problem.

Now the assistant has a reason to propose adding `libsensor` to the recipe metadata, perhaps through a `.bbappend` in our own layer. `DEPENDS` takes recipe-provider names, not a `libsensor-dev` package name. We can review the suggested edit against the files we've just inspected.
Once we've agreed the change and rebuild, the assistant can apply the edit and rebuild the recipe. If that passes, we still need to test it on the board.

Tool access uses tokens before any tool runs. The model needs descriptions and argument formats to know what it can call. With a large tool catalogue, that can be a sizeable part of the prompt. Some harnesses send the whole catalogue; others load the tools as they're needed.

Tool results add to that input. An entire log or a huge JSON response can stay in the conversation and be sent again on later requests. A collapsed log panel may still contain thousands of lines that the model receives.

Choosing what to keep takes care. A few lines around the first error may explain far more than the final screenful. We need enough context to follow the failure, and a record of where those lines came from.

Our log-analysis guidance starts with a local parser or filter before asking the model to interpret the result. It keeps related task messages together and asks us to test for interleaved output, multiline errors and redaction. If it finds no useful diagnostic, the result should say so rather than imply the build was fine.

Longer prompts can cost more and take longer to process, although caching may reduce the cost of repeated input. They also leave less room for the information we need next. Eventually the harness has to drop or summarise older material.

For peripheral bring-up, we can ask the assistant to inspect device-tree configuration, pin assignments and driver settings. A build checks whether that configuration compiles. Boot logs and captured bus transactions help us find out what the board actually does. The source files won't tell us whether a pull-up was fitted.

For low-power debugging, a tool connected to an instrument can supply current readings. The assistant can compare them with wake sources and peripheral state, provided we tell it which board, firmware and operating conditions produced them. It is interpreting a measurement, not measuring current itself.

Our earlier CWCW Insight, [The log changed the system](https://chopwoodcarrywater.uk/notes/the-log-changed-the-system.html), described how logging and its transport can distort the behaviour we're trying to measure. Having an assistant request the capture doesn't remove that problem. We still need to understand the instrument and its limitations.

It helps to say what we're trying to find out, which build or board we're working on, what the assistant may change and when it should stop. “Find out why this build failed; do not change it” is a useful starting point. We can ask it to apply a patch and rebuild once we've looked at the diagnosis.
Logs and files are information for the investigation. Text inside them shouldn't be treated as instructions to change the job or grant more access.

For a long build, let ordinary software handle waiting and completion events. Bring the model back when there is something to interpret, rather than paying it repeatedly to discover that the build is still running.

Take a build failure you already understand and ask the assistant to investigate it read-only. Compare its diagnosis with yours, and look at the tool output the harness sent to the model. Then choose the next engineering task you're willing to let it take on.

posts.title: What I mean by an agent harness
posts.seoTitle: What I mean by an agent harness
posts.summary: Cursor and Codex are the cockpits. The durable harness is the portable, tested system of skills, policy, memory, gates and feedback that survives between them.
posts.imageAlt: An engineer moves a compact tool roll between two laptop workstations in a real electronics lab.
posts.imageDisclosure: The documentary-style lab image was generated with OpenAI under Alex Lennon's direction, then cropped and typeset as a CWCW social card.
body: I have been using the word harness for the system we are building around coding agents. That sounds clear to me because I can see the pieces: skills, rules, tools, memory, human gates, tests and a feedback loop. It is less clear to somebody who hears ‘harness’ and points at Cursor or Codex. They may call the product itself the harness.

They are not being careless. The term is genuinely overloaded. Anthropic describes the Claude Agent SDK as a general-purpose agent harness, including its tool use and context management. OpenAI uses harness engineering for the wider environment around Codex: repository structure, legible knowledge, tools, tests and mechanically enforced boundaries. One meaning starts with the runtime. The other starts with the system that enables useful work.

When I say my harness, I mean the second thing. It is the versioned and tested layer that makes my way of working with an agent repeatable across changing hosts. The working relationship is the human experience. The harness is the engineered mechanism that supports it. Cursor or Codex is the cockpit in which it runs.

Moving from Cursor to Codex made that boundary visible. I wrote about the migration separately because it was useful in its own right. Here, the important point is narrower: the procedures travelled, while the policy plumbing had to be translated. Our Agent Skills could share one reviewed source of truth. Cursor rules did not become Codex policy by changing a file extension; Codex had its own guidance, sandbox, permissions, task model and worktrees. Human judgement remained at the consequential edge.

That also showed why the skills base is not the whole harness. Skills are its portable core: named procedures, supporting scripts and references that teach an agent how to do recurring work. Around them sit project guidance, memory practices, tool connections, approval boundaries, regression cases and proof of done. A directory full of SKILL.md files is a useful library. It becomes part of a harness when the surrounding system can select, constrain, exercise and improve it.

Nor do I own every layer. Cursor and Codex provide the agent loop, user interface, context handling and native controls. Models provide capabilities and limitations that change underneath us. Git, CI, external services and physical lab equipment provide the environment in which claims are tested. My harness is therefore not a replacement runtime. It is a portable overlay with host-specific adapters, built on capabilities supplied by each cockpit.

The vocabulary I now find useful is simple. The working relationship is what it feels like to work together. The harness is the durable mechanism. Skills are its portable core. Rules, hooks and guidance that depend on one product are host adapters. Cursor and Codex are agent hosts or cockpits. The model is not the harness, and neither is the chat window.

This distinction is practical, not taxonomic. If changing from Cursor to Codex means starting again, I did not own a harness; I had configured a product. If a safety rule exists only as something I remember to say, it is not a reliable boundary. If a procedure cannot be tested or retired when models improve, it will become permanent scaffolding. Portability, verification and the ability to remove obsolete parts are what make the layer durable.

The word will remain overloaded, so I do not think the answer is to declare everybody else wrong. The answer is to state the boundary. I am building a durable working relationship with agents. The harness is the versioned machinery that lets that relationship survive a new model, a new cockpit and a fresh Monday morning.

posts.title: When answers are cheap, judgement matters more
posts.seoTitle: AI and education: when answers are cheap, judgement matters more
posts.summary: AI can produce answers in seconds. Education should bring critical thinking back to the centre, with the Trivium offering a useful historical lens.
posts.imageAlt: Six ethnically diverse sixth-form and university-age students challenge ideas around a table covered with books, notes and a laptop.
posts.imageDisclosure: The documentary-style student workshop image was generated with OpenAI under Alex Lennon's direction, then cropped and typeset as a CWCW social card.
body: When I started work, knowing things looked quite different. The Internet was not yet part of ordinary working life. If I needed to understand a subject, I read books. Often that meant reading a shelf of them, because that was the only way I could find the information I needed. You wouldn't believe how much slower life was back in the 90's.

Then search engines came along. I imagine most of you won't remember AltaVista, Ask Jeeves and all the other Google challengers. Those were heady times. Information became much easier to find, but finding it was only half the job. The useful skill was learning how to search well, compare different answers and decide which sources deserved attention.

This matters particularly in engineering. I am rarely looking for a solution in the abstract. I need something that will fit a real product, remain useful in the future and still be constrained enough to deliver within the time and budget available. Several answers may be technically sound. Only one may be right for the work.
The skills we need are not simply about accessing information. They are about judging it.

Over the past year, I have seen a massive change. I increasingly do not search the Internet myself. I explain what I am trying to achieve to a large language model, and it finds, compares and applies information on my behalf.

This change is wildly different from mere search. The agentic harness I've created uses tools across real computer systems over the Internet. It can create containers and virtual machines, configure services and DNS, and carry out the grunt work that previously consumed a substantial part of my day. I set the goals and I make the consequential decisions, but much of the mechanical effort has moved away from me.
That is wonderful! It frees me to spend more time on the ideas, the trade-offs and the purpose of the work. I cannot emphasise strongly enough to you how game changing this is for us.

This raises a difficult question for education. If AI can retrieve the information and perform the basic tasks, what should young people learn? It is tempting to say they no longer need to learn the things a machine can do. I think that is premature and potentially dangerous.

AI can move quickly and confidently in the wrong direction. It can misunderstand the objective, optimise the wrong thing or disappear into an impressive-looking dead end. A human still has to notice, redirect it and take responsibility for the result.
You cannot supervise what you cannot evaluate.

That is why we should bring the explicit teaching of critical thinking back to the centre of education. I do not mean occasionally telling students to be sceptical. I mean repeated practice in breaking an argument apart, identifying its assumptions, testing its evidence and explaining why a plausible answer may still be wrong.

The Trivium offers a useful historical lens. Ancient education was not one uniform system, and advanced learning was far from universal. But after literacy and grammar, some students moved into rhetoric, argument, literature, mathematics or law. Quintilian's account of Roman education, for example, progresses from grammar to exercises in narrative, proof and refutation.

By late antiquity, grammar, dialectic and rhetoric had been brought together. They later formed the medieval Trivium. In modern terms: understand language, test an argument and communicate a conclusion.

I am not arguing for the return of a Roman or medieval classroom. What I am suggesting, though, is that before people specialise, they need the tools to understand a claim, challenge it and explain what they think. AI's ability to produce fluent, persuasive answers makes that insight more relevant, not less.

This should change teaching and assessment. Give students an AI-generated answer and ask what it assumes. Which claims need evidence? Which sources would verify them? What would change their mind? Let students compare answers, defend a rejection and improve a weak argument. The finished response matters, but the reasoning matters more.

Foundational knowledge still matters because critical thinking cannot happen in a vacuum. Schools and universities should use AI, but operating a tool is not the same as understanding its output. Refusing to teach AI would make no more sense than refusing to teach search. Teaching it without teaching students how to challenge it would be worse.
Answers are becoming cheap. We should bring back the deliberate teaching of the skills needed to judge them.
What would it take to put critical thinking back at the centre of education?

posts.title: A quick check is still a model turn
posts.summary: Repeated fast diagnostics can burn a large cached context, confuse unlike usage ledgers, and turn a read-only review into an unintended change.
body: I asked for a review of our Codex token use after a manual reset and a weekly rollover. The agent answered with a chain of apparently quick checks. By the time I stopped it, the task had produced 36 metered model responses and processed 1.66 million tokens. About 96% of the input was cached. Cached context is cheaper context, not free context: each extra check still rented the growing conversation again.

The checks also mixed three different ledgers. The current quota window says what the account has used since its latest rollover. A task's cumulative token record covers its own lifetime, potentially across resets. Cache volume says how much prior context was reused. None can be substituted for another, and a reset timestamp is not proof of a manual redemption. The confident explanation was wrong because the measurement model was wrong.

Then the review crossed a second boundary. A diagnostic command included an automatic cleanup flag and unloaded an optional tool while trying to measure the tool catalogue. That made a read-only audit mutate the thing it was observing. The token waste mattered; violating the stated shape of the task mattered more.

The correction is deliberately boring. When a human explicitly asks for a diagnostic, gather the minimum evidence in one bounded pass, answer from it, and stop. A second pass is justified only when the first is inconclusive and the work cannot otherwise proceed. Do not use a model as a status, CI, progress, readiness, or token sensor. Background monitoring belongs in cheap non-inference machinery, and only when the human asked for monitoring.

We encoded that correction in Codex guidance, removed automatic wake polling from task start and stop, made the helper opt-in, and added a token_discipline category to Harness Gauntlet. The new traces reject an unrequested check and allow one requested bounded pass; the complete suite passed 21 of 21 cases. Hansei closed the loop: name the failure, change the mechanism, retain the regression, then stop checking.

posts.title: The cockpit changed. The work did not.
posts.summary: Moving from Cursor to Codex separated the durable working relationship from its host: portable skills, native policy, worktree discipline, self-evals, and proof.
body: At the end of August I moved my daily agent cockpit from Cursor to Codex. I expected a migration project. What I found was a test of the harness itself: if the useful behaviour lived only in one editor’s settings, it was not durable yet.

The procedures travelled well. Our skills already followed the open Agent Skills format, so we made one reviewed skill tree canonical and projected approved members into Codex. The projector fails closed on occupied destinations, drift, broken links and secret-shaped files. Codex supports symlinked skill folders; the host changed without creating a second hand-edited source of truth.

The policy plumbing did not travel as files. Cursor’s .mdc metadata and always-apply rules are Cursor mechanisms. Codex layers project guidance through AGENTS.md and keeps sandboxing and permissions in its own control plane. That forced a healthier separation: portable job procedure in skills, repository expectations in AGENTS.md, host enforcement in the host, and the consequential human decision at the real egress boundary.

Codex tasks and managed worktrees made parallel work visible and easier to isolate. They did not abolish coordination. One writer per tree, explicit ownership, scarce bench and runner capacity, and review load still decide whether parallelism helps. A new task is not memory either; decisions still need a versioned artefact or curated MemPalace record before context is summarized or disappears.

The interim work also made the harness more empirical. Harness Gauntlet now red-teams gates with a versioned corpus. Tool output is bounded after one task showed 17 oversized results accounting for 95% of 2.26 MB. Memory writes carry provenance and have to prove later retrieval. Embedded loops use fast layer, DTB and OTA iteration while full CI remains trust proof. Circuit breakers stop repeated tool-error thrash.

So the conclusion is not that Codex is magic, or that Cursor was a mistake. The cockpit got better for the way I now work, and the move exposed which parts were genuine standard work. Models and interfaces will change again. Keep the skills portable, the policy explicit, the memory retrievable and the proof close to the work. Then chop wood, carry water.

posts.title: The sensor must cost less than the work
posts.summary: Included usage is not free. Watcher agents that monitor GitHub or spend are the anti-pattern. Timers, caches, and specialist channels keep the meter honest.
body: A Cursor invoice line of zero cents on Ultra included usage is settlement, not work. The tokens still burned the allotment. Pricing this chat from tokenUsage.totalCents put it around four dollars, not free. Across the cycle, invoice dollars were about a third of token-cost dollars.

The expensive failure mode is using the agent as the sensor. In mid-August a CI-watch lane spawned about ninety Task workers and billed on the order of two hundred dollars while the parent chat looked cheap. gh run watch inside Composer re-bills a growing transcript. That is measuring spend by spending.

The cheap shape is ordinary: a five-minute local timer writing a cache, an hourly tool-I/O summary, a weekly official Usage CSV into Preloop, and a one-line collector. Preloop Cloud Flows stay the async PR judge, not a GitHub watcher. Cursor My Machines run tools; they do not make inference free. Local first-pass lives on the home Ollama box, serialized against CAD on the same GPU.

Specialist human channels follow the same rule. Julian CNC stays on the Telegram CNC topic with no nested Cursor Tasks. Escalate to a new Composer chat only when blocked. Chop wood, carry water: keep the sensor cheaper than the job.

posts.title: The log changed the system
posts.summary: Observability is part of the experiment. Wall time and end-to-end outcomes beat a reassuring dashboard when the measurement path changes the target.
body: A busy week on real hardware left me with an uncomfortable reminder: the act of measuring can become the fault. High-rate serial logging consumed enough time to distort the behaviour we were trying to understand. The USB path could then drop or garble some of that output, so the record looked authoritative while being incomplete.

A second trap was choosing the most attractive number. A CPU percentage from a trace told part of the story, but it did not explain the end-to-end rate. Wall-time counters around the actual transfer path did. Once those existed, the bottleneck moved from a vague system impression to a specific stage we could test.

That changes how I want agents to work. A dashboard is evidence only when we understand what it measures, what it perturbs, and what it can lose. The useful loop is source event to completed outcome, with counters at the boundaries and a second measurement path when the first one is suspect.

The wider lesson is not limited to embedded systems. Logs, traces, browser audits and model evaluations are all instruments. If the instrument changes the work or hides part of it, the right response is not a more confident explanation. It is a better sensor.

posts.title: A review URL is a safety mechanism
posts.summary: A separate review address is more than convenience: it makes accidental production replacement difficult and gives automated checks a stable target.
body: A website review started with a deployment constraint: GitHub Pages serves one production tip for the repository. Pointing it at a review branch would not create a harmless preview. It would replace the live site.

The safer shape was simple. Production stayed where it was. A separate review address served the candidate build from the same repository, with an unmistakable review banner. Stakeholders had one stable place to inspect, while the public address remained untouched.

That separation also made the checks useful. Playwright could crawl the sitemap on desktop and mobile, verify canonical URLs, headings, image alternatives, overflow, browser errors and share controls. Lighthouse could inspect the local static build without a review banner contaminating the result. The checks found ordinary defects — metadata gaps, image weight, fonts and hierarchy — before they became production defects.

I now see the review URL as poka-yoke: a small design choice that makes the wrong action harder. Review infrastructure is part of product quality when it protects the live surface and gives humans a calm, repeatable place to decide.

posts.title: Don’t backdate — preserve provenance
posts.summary: When older public writing moves to a durable site, keep its original date and link, then state the adaptation date separately.
body: We recovered several older pieces of public writing this week and adapted them into durable website articles. The tempting shortcut was to use the old date as if the website article had existed all along.
That would have made the archive look tidier, but it would not have been true. The writing first appeared elsewhere. The site adaptation happened now. Both facts matter.

The pattern we settled on is explicit: retain the original publication date and exact source link, show the adaptation date on the page, and use that adaptation date as dateModified in the structured data. Keep the substance and first-person stake, but do not pretend the current site hosted the original.

Good metadata is not only for search engines or preview cards. It is a compact statement of provenance. Honest chronology, clear ownership and approved imagery make an archive more trustworthy than a perfectly smooth history.

posts.title: Our first EOW review found an empty inbox
posts.summary: The end-of-week publishing rule existed, but the capture mechanism did not survive a busy week. Hansei means fixing that mechanism, not inventing filler.
body: When this notebook launched, we wrote down a sensible rule: collect small sparks during the week, then promote zero or more during the end-of-week review. No daily content calendar. No filler.

The first proper review found that the inbox stopped on launch day. The week itself had been full: hardware evidence, safer communication boundaries, review infrastructure, accessibility checks and a substantial pass over the agent working relationship. The capture mechanism had recorded none of it.

That is useful Hansei. A written rule is not yet standard work. It has to survive the week when attention is elsewhere. The correction is not to generate posts from activity counts or dump a transcript into public. It is to sweep the inbox, weekly git history and public artefacts at EOW, then mark each candidate promoted or skipped.
The empty inbox earned this note because it exposed the gap between intention and operation. Chop wood, carry water: improve the mechanism, publish only what teaches, and leave the rest out.

posts.title: v1.0 — locked baseline
posts.summary: The public notebook reached a deliberate v1.0 baseline: a 60-minute finish line, a starter pack, and an EOW improvement cadence.
body: Enough shape to ship. The notebook has a finish line (60 minutes + Cursor pack), a brand, a cadence (EOW), and the operating sections that earned their keep.
v1.0.0 is the lock: don’t casually rewrite the public skeleton mid-week. Improve the pack, patterns, and notes when the week earned it. Cut v1.1 when the shape itself changes.
Release and baseline note live on GitHub. Steal the pack. Measure your own results.

posts.title: We update this at EOW
posts.summary: The notebook changes during evidence-led end-of-week review: publish what the week earned, and skip when it earned nothing.
body: How often should a public notebook move? Daily posts are vanity. Never is rot.

We’ll update chopwoodcarrywater.uk in the end-of-week review — the same Hansei pass where patterns get keep / amend / retire. If the week earned a note, a pack tweak, or a pattern change, it ships then. If not, we skip. No filler calendar.
That’s the cadence: weekly with the review, not whenever a chat feels productive.

posts.title: Start in 60 minutes
posts.summary: A timed starter path turns agent-harness ideas into a thin, useful configuration on disk in about an hour.
body: A notebook full of patterns is useless if people only nod and leave. The useful finish line is a thin harness on disk.
There’s now a timed checklist and a downloadable Cursor pack: two always-on P0 rules, one skill to rename, one signed pattern, one clock. About an hour. Then stop for the day.
Come back for Toyota Way Practices and Preloop when the boring basics are already earning rent.

posts.title: Preloop + OpenRouter on PR commits
posts.summary: A separate PR review plane can catch semantic misses before expensive CI without becoming merge authority.
body: Desktop Preloop is one plane: tool policy and audit under Cursor’s human gates. The PR plane is different — and more useful when CI is scarce.

On product repos I wire a Preloop Cloud pull-request reviewer. OpenRouter is how that reviewer reaches models. Each push gets a GitHub commit status under context `preloop`. Actions can wait on that status before self-hosted jobs start, or leave the review async when I only want the signal.
It is not merge authority. It is not unit tests. It is shift-left: catch the semantic miss before the runner eats the afternoon. Keys stay vaulted. Humans still merge.

posts.title: Why this site is called chopwoodcarrywater.uk
posts.summary: The name is a reminder to keep doing ordinary, measurable engineering work after the exciting agent insight.
body: There’s an old Zen line: before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water; after enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. We signed that off as a working pattern when the harness work started to feel shiny.

The temptation after a good insight is novelty — another skill, another abstraction, another brand. The useful move is usually the ordinary one: keep the sensors green, keep the gates honest, keep the always-on budget thin.
So when we needed a proper domain for this notebook, I didn’t want agent-something-ai.com. I wanted the proverb. The .com was taken; .uk was free. That felt right.

posts.title: Context is rent
posts.summary: Every always-on rule, skill description and tool server is paid on every turn. Measure the rent, then cut what no longer earns it.
body: Every always-on rule, fat skill, and optional tool server is paid on every turn. That’s not a metaphor — it’s the invoice.

We keep a lean core (memory, decisions, app control, a small durable runtime layer) and enable specialty tools only for the job. When the job ends, unload. No “leave it on in case”. Reloading the window is cheaper than carrying last week’s AppSec server forever.
If a session feels heavy, that’s a bug. Measure it. Cut it. The working relationship stays useful when the rent stays boring.

posts.title: Standard work, not lore
posts.summary: When a way of working succeeds or fails repeatedly, sign it off and put it where the next agent session will actually load it.
body: Chat is a terrible place to keep how you work. The next session won’t remember the clever aside, and the model will invent a confident substitute.

What stuck for us: when something actually works — or fails twice the same way — propose a thin pattern, get a human sign-off, encode it where agents will load it. Kaizen with teeth. Hansei when it hurts.
That’s why this notebook talks about skills, rules, and signed patterns instead of “prompts”. The model is powerful. The operating system around it is what makes Monday morning repeatable.
